$comment: Golden contract fixture for the MCP daemon's GET /health (mt#4322). Sibling of cockpit-health-shape.json (mt#2629), which pins the COCKPIT's health route — these are two different services with two different bodies and must not be conflated. Asserted by src/mcp/health-payload.test.ts against `buildMcpHealthResponse`, the same function `src/commands/mcp/start-command.ts`'s route calls. See contract/README.md.
consumedBy: src/mcp/setup/local-http-apply.ts (classifyDaemonProbe — reads `ready`, falling back to `persistence.mode` for daemons built before mt#4297)
src/mcp/daemon/local-daemon.ts (adopt-or-fail — asserts `service: "minsky-mcp"` before adopting a port holder)
src/cockpit/widgets/mcp-server-status.ts (HOSTED_MCP_SERVICE — the hosted server's identity assertion)
docs/local-mcp-daemon.md (the operator-facing description of this surface)
.github/workflows/bundle-boot-smoke.yml (asserts a 200 within 30s; does NOT read this body)

cockpit-tray/src-tauri/src/supervisor/daemon_core.rs (probe_health / parse_health_body — reads `service` for identity and keeps the whole body for policy-specific fields; its `is_ours` deliberately does NOT key on the status code)

cockpit-tray/src-tauri/src/supervisor.rs (the DB-degraded policy and its DB_DEGRADED_POLL_THRESHOLD — cockpit-only until mt#4479 gave the MCP daemon a `db` field of the same shape; mt#4472 owns generalizing it)
src/mcp/daemon/control.ts (mt#4466's `minsky mcp status` — reads `db`/`dbCheck` when present and falls back to `ready` + `persistence.reason` when they are not)
$readyFieldNote: mt#4297 added `ready`; mt#4322 pinned it. `ready` answers READINESS ('can this daemon serve DB-backed work?'), which is a different question from the LIVENESS the status code answers ('did the process boot?'). They diverge in exactly one case and that divergence is deliberate: `persistence.mode === "unconfigured"` is reported HEALTHY (200, `status: "ok"`) because it is the expected local/dev/offline boot path AND the exact state `bundle-boot-smoke` asserts a 200 against — while `ready` is false, because every DB-backed call would fail. A consumer that infers readiness from the status code reintroduces the incident this field exists to make visible: a shared daemon served 200 with no persistence provider for 31 hours, and `minsky setup local-http` would have pointed every conversation at it, because 'a Minsky daemon answered' was the whole test. Do NOT derive the status code from `ready`, and do NOT derive readiness from the status code.
$conditionalFieldsNote: mt#4479 added `db` and `dbCheck`. They are CONDITIONAL, not required — emitted only when `persistence.mode === "connected"`, so the `unconfigured` and `unavailable` bodies stay byte-identical to what they emitted before and the exact-key-set assertion above keeps holding for them. They are a MACHINE-READABLE rendering of the same `ReadinessResult` that decides `ready`; nothing here is new information, it is information that was only available as prose inside `persistence.reason`. The consumer that needs the difference is Rust in a 5s poll loop (cockpit-tray/src-tauri/src/supervisor.rs), which would otherwise regex a sentence written for a human. `db` uses the cockpit's own key name deliberately (contract/cockpit-health-shape.json): that file's DB-degraded policy is CockpitPolicy-only for exactly one stated reason — verbatim, 'only the cockpit's /api/health publishes a `db` field' — so matching the key is what lets one policy read both daemons. Only `ok` and `degraded` are emitted; the cockpit's third value `unreachable` is unrepresentable here because the `connected` precondition already means a provider is wired. TRAP, stated because the obvious reading is wrong: `dbCheck.checkedAt` ADVANCES on every poll, INCLUDING when a previous probe is still outstanding — `assessProbeOutcome` stamps it on all four branches. A stale `checkedAt` is therefore NOT a wedge signal. The wedge signal is `persistence.reason` (which names `outstandingForMs`) or `dbCheck.durationMs`.
$dbCheckDivergenceNote: PR #3277 R1. `dbCheck` shares its NAME with the cockpit's (contract/cockpit-health-shape.json) and its MEMBERS do not mean the same things — a reader who assumes symmetry gets both wrong, so the divergence is stated here rather than left to be discovered. (1) `durationMs` is deliberately NOT named `latencyMs`: the cockpit's `latencyMs` is the round-trip of the last SUCCESSFUL probe and is not reset when a later probe fails, so it can sit non-null beside a degraded `db`, describing a last-good measurement rather than the current state; ours is how long THIS check took however it settled, including a timeout. A 43-second timeout emitted under the name `latencyMs` would read to a cross-daemon consumer as a healthy round-trip. A different meaning gets a different name. (2) `checkedAt` shares its name AND has the OPPOSITE behaviour: the cockpit deliberately does not restamp it while a probe is outstanding, so a stale value there IS the wedge signal, whereas `assessProbeOutcome` stamps it on all four branches here, so it always advances. Only `db` itself is safe to read symmetrically across the two daemons — `ok`/`degraded` mean the same thing on both, which is exactly what makes that shared key worth having.
$fieldGroupSplitNote: PR #3277 R1 asked whether splitting the schema across `conditionalFields` and `dbCheckFields` is ad-hoc duplication. It follows this file's existing convention rather than inventing one: `persistenceFields` already declares the members of the `persistence` sub-object separately from the top-level `fields` map, and `dbCheckFields` does the same for `dbCheck`. Both ARE validated — src/mcp/health-payload.test.ts iterates `conditionalFields` and `dbCheckFields` and asserts each declared member's type against the emitted body, and a separate assertion pins the emitted key set to `fields` + `conditionalFields` in BOTH directions, so a field added to the emitter without updating this file fails here, and a field declared here that the emitter does not send fails too. `conditionalFields` has to be separate from `fields` for a mechanical reason: `fields` is asserted as an EXACT key set against the unconditional bodies, so listing a conditional field there would break the unconfigured and unavailable cases.
$readyProbeNote: mt#4471 changed what `ready` is DERIVED FROM, without changing this shape — no field was added, renamed or retyped, so every consumer listed above is unaffected structurally. It was `persistence.mode === "connected"`, which is a claim about the provider's TYPE (`provider.getCapabilities().sql`, a static declaration); it is now that precondition AND an observed round trip against the pool, bounded at 1500ms. The change is that `ready` can now be FALSE while `mode` is `"connected"` — a value combination this body could not previously emit, and the one the 2026-08-23 outage needed: a SQL-capable provider whose pool had stopped serving, while /health answered `ready: true` twice across 45 minutes and three dead conversations. When that combination is emitted, `persistence.reason` carries the probe's explanation. The 1500ms bound is derived from the tray supervisor's own 2s HTTP request timeout (cockpit-tray/src-tauri/src/supervisor.rs), NOT from its 5s poll interval: a probe that outlives the request budget makes the daemon read as DOWN rather than NOT-READY, and those two states have opposite recoveries.
$readyFallbackNote: mt#4297's consumer-side tolerance is load-bearing and must survive any change here. `classifyDaemonProbe` in src/mcp/setup/local-http-apply.ts reads `ready` WHEN PRESENT and falls back to `persistence.mode` otherwise, because keying on `ready` alone would classify EVERY daemon built before mt#4297 as not-ready — including during the rollout window, which turns a safety check into an outage. So `ready` is required in THIS fixture (the current emitter always sends it) while the consumer stays tolerant of its absence. Those are not in conflict: the fixture pins what this build EMITS, the fallback covers what an OLDER build emits, and a consumer talking to a daemon it did not build cannot assume they match.
$serviceFieldNote: mt#3148: `service` is the uniform identity key every Minsky service emits, and it is what makes a health probe able to FAIL. Every Minsky service is built from the same monorepo, so a misconfigured build can put a DIFFERENT application on the host and it answers 200 exactly like the right one (mt#3142: the MCP server served the reviewer's host for ~1h while every reviewer route 404'd, and the status-code check stayed green throughout). Assert this field, not merely the status code. `server` ("Minsky MCP Server") is retained UNCHANGED alongside it rather than replaced: mt#3142's own diagnosis read `server`, and mem#704's probe recipe still cites it.
$transportFieldNote: Hardcoded "http" and correct by construction: this route only exists on the HTTP transport, since the stdio transport serves no HTTP surface at all. It is NOT derived from the transport resolution mt#4322 single-sourced — a stdio process never reaches this code. Recorded because the constant looks like a candidate for that refactor and is deliberately not one.
$persistenceFieldNote: `persistence.mode` is one of connected / unconfigured / unavailable (packages/domain/src/persistence/health.ts). `reason` is present ONLY when the assessment supplies one, so a consumer must treat it as optional — which is why it is absent from `persistenceFields` above rather than typed as a required string. `unavailable` is the only mode that flips the status code to 503: it means a Postgres connection WAS configured and initialization failed (a genuine outage), as distinct from `unconfigured`, which means none was configured at all.
